author.name: William Shakespeare
author.biography: Shakespeare left Stratford-upon-Avon for a career in London's theatres, where he worked as an actor, playwright and company shareholder. He knew stories as things people performed before other people, with attention, sympathy and judgment changing from moment to moment. Shakespeare wrote Richard through the historical inheritance of the Tudor period. His theatrical invention makes the audience's attraction to a persuasive performance part of the problem of political power.

hook.text: Why is it so tempting to enjoy a villain who lets you in on the plan?

paragraphs: Richard tells the audience what he intends to do, and then goes to work. He can be witty, intimate and startlingly effective. People onstage struggle to understand him while we enjoy being admitted to his confidence.

That privileged position is uncomfortable. Knowing a manipulation is happening does not prevent us from admiring its execution. Shakespeare makes spectators feel the seduction of competence: the person pursuing a terrible aim may also be the liveliest intelligence in the room.

The play surrounds that energy with the people whose losses it creates. Memory and grief resist the speed with which an ambitious ruler wants to move on. The theatrical Richard is a dramatic construction, not an impartial biography of the historical king.
Read for when complicity stops feeling like cleverness. What does the pleasure of understanding a ruthless person make us overlook about everyone else?

orientation.text: Family claims follow the Wars of the Roses. A brief genealogy helps, but Richard's direct addresses make his immediate schemes clear. Distinguish the play from historical biography.
